Today, President Biden is issuing a landmark Executive Order to ensure that America leads the way in seizing the promise and managing the risks of artificial intelligence (AI). The Executive Order establishes new standards for AI safety and security, protects Americans’ privacy, advances equity and civil rights, stands up for consumers and workers, promotes innovation and competition, advances American leadership around the world, and more.

As part of the Biden-Harris Administration’s comprehensive strategy for responsible innovation, the Executive Order builds on previous actions the President has taken, including work that led to voluntary commitments from 15 leading companies to drive safe, secure, and trustworthy development of AI.

The Executive Order directs the following actions:

**New Standards for AI Safety and Security**

As AI’s capabilities grow, so do its implications for Americans’ safety and security. **With this Executive Order, the****President directs the****most sweeping****actions****ever taken****to protect Americans from****the potential****risks****of****AI****systems****:**

* **Require that developers of the most powerful AI systems share their safety test results and other critical information with the U.S. government.**In accordance with the Defense Production Act, the Order will require that companies developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests. These measures will ensure AI systems are safe, secure, and trustworthy before companies make them public.
* **Develop standards, tools, and tests to help ensure that AI systems are safe, secure, and trustworthy.** The National Institute of Standards and Technology will set the rigorous standards for extensive red-team testing to ensure safety before public release. The Department of Homeland Security will apply those standards to critical infrastructure sectors and establish the AI Safety and Security Board. The Departments of Energy and Homeland Security will also address AI systems’ threats to critical infrastructure, as well as chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity risks. Together, these are the most significant actions ever taken by any government to advance the field of AI safety.
* **Protect against the risks of using AI to engineer dangerous biological materials**by developing strong new standards for biological synthesis screening. Agencies that fund life-science projects will establish these standards as a condition of federal funding, creating powerful incentives to ensure appropriate screening and manage risks potentially made worse by AI.
* **Protect Americans from AI-enabled fraud and deception by establishing standards and best practices for detecting AI-generated content and authenticating official content**. The Department of Commerce will develop guidance for content authentication and watermarking to clearly label AI-generated content. Federal agencies will use these tools to make it easy for Americans to know that the communications they receive from their government are authentic—and set an example for the private sector and governments around the world.
* **Establish an advanced cybersecurity program to develop AI tools to find and fix vulnerabilities in critical software,**building on the Biden-Harris Administration’s ongoing AI Cyber Challenge. Together, these efforts will harness AI’s potentially game-changing cyber capabilities to make software and networks more secure.
* **Order the development of a National Security Memorandum that directs further actions on AI and security,**to be developed by the National Security Council and White House Chief of Staff. This document will ensure that the United States military and intelligence community use AI safely, ethically, and effectively in their missions, and will direct actions to counter adversaries’ military use of AI.

**Protecting Americans’ Privacy**

Without safeguards, AI can put Americans’ privacy further at risk. **New START**[[c]](#cite_note-5) was a [nuclear arms reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament") [treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty "Treaty") between the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") with the formal name of ***Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms***. It was signed on 8 April 2010 in [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague"),[[3]](#cite_note-Lee-6)[[4]](#cite_note-7) and after [ratification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratification "Ratification")[[5]](#cite_note-csmonitor.com-8)[[6]](#cite_note-af.reuters.com-9) it [entered into force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entry_into_force "Entry into force") on 5 February 2011.[[1]](#cite_note-USA_Today/The_Associated_Press-1)

New START replaced the Treaty of [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") ([SORT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SORT "SORT")), which was to expire in December 2012. It followed the [START I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_I "START I") treaty, which expired in December 2009; the proposed [START II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_II "START II") treaty which never entered into force; and the [START III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_III "START III") treaty, for which negotiations were never concluded.

The treaty called for halving the number of [strategic nuclear missile launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile "Intercontinental ballistic missile"). It also called for the establishment of a new inspection and verification regime, replacing the SORT mechanism. It did not limit the number of operationally inactive [nuclear warheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_stockpile "Nuclear stockpile") that can be stockpiled, a number in the high thousands.[[7]](#cite_note-10)

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 1B.1 Research Note

**Lens:** 1B.1 — Did the ruler seek to reduce nuclear or other existential risk, rather than increase prestige, leverage, or personal power through escalation?

**Summary of evidence:** Biden's 2023 record on nuclear/existential risk is mixed. The single most consequential existential-risk action of 2023 was the **Oct 30 Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI** — the broadest national AI governance framework to date, with explicit mandates on AI-driven chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) risks. On arms control, however, the U.S. entered 2023 already constrained: **Russia suspended participation in New START on Feb 21, 2023**, leaving the strategic-arms framework with no inspections and no data exchange for the remainder of Biden's term. The administration continued nuclear modernization (GBSD/Sentinel, B61-12, Columbia-class, W93 warhead) — actions critics frame as escalation via capability, supporters frame as deterrence necessity.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Russia suspended New START on Feb 21, 2023

- **Title / source:** New START (Wikipedia article, citing Russian state Duma and Reuters)
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Article reflects event Feb 21, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START
- **Summary:** "On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START. However, it did not withdraw from the treaty, and clarified that it would continue to abide by the numerical limits in the treaty." New START was the only remaining U.S.–Russia treaty limiting deployed strategic warheads (1,550 ceiling) and launchers. Suspension meant no on-site inspections, no data exchanges, and no notifications of strategic forces movements — eroding transparency and predictability precisely as the war in Ukraine entered a grinding second year.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.1 (existential-risk reduction: Biden was on the defensive; he did not cause the suspension but could not reverse it)
- **Also informs:** 8B.4 (foreign-policy leadership), 8B.6 (crisis response), 8B.7 (rule of law / international norms on arms control)

### Claim 2 — AI Executive Order (Oct 30, 2023) addressed CBRN and nuclear-relevant AI risks

- **Title / source:** "Fact Sheet: President Biden Issues Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence"
- **Publisher:** The White House (Biden administration archive)
- **Date:** October 30, 2023
- **URL:** https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2023/10/30/fact-sheet-president-biden-issues-executive-order-on-safe-secure-and-trustworthy-artificial-intelligence/
- **Summary:** The EO invokes the Defense Production Act to require developers of frontier models that "pose a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety" to notify the federal government when training the model and to share red-team safety test results. It directs the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security to "address AI systems' threats to critical infrastructure, as well as chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity risks" — explicitly naming nuclear alongside other CBRN threats. - **Direct question ID:** 1B.1 (the EO is the year's clearest pro-risk-reduction action — it imposes safety, reporting, and testing requirements on the technology class many existential-risk analysts view as a top-tier civilizational threat, and specifically references nuclear risks)

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 1B.1

- **No new strategic-arms treaty.** Russia suspended New START on Feb 21, 2023; Biden did not achieve a follow-on framework. The 2026 expiry of New START removed the last bilateral limit on U.S. and Russian deployed strategic warheads — a core 1B.1 regression that began on Biden's watch.
- **Failure to ratify CTBT.** The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty remained unratified by the U.S. in 2023, leaving the global test-moratorium regime on voluntary status.
- **Modernization lock-in.** Continued full funding of the Sentinel ICBM, B61-12, W93, Columbia-class, and B-21 programs signal long-term escalation-by-capability commitments rather than disarmament.
- **Cluster-munitions transfer.** Supply of cluster munitions to a combatant in 2023, bypassing the global norm codified by the CCM.
- **Taiwan-comment escalation.** Repeated explicit commitments to defend Taiwan, framed by Beijing as escalation.
- **AI risk reduction was unilateral.** The Oct 30 EO was U.S.-only; major frontier-AI labs in the U.S. were bound, but no analogous regime bound Chinese or Russian AI development.

## Favorable evidence on 1B.1

- **AI EO as landmark risk reduction.** The Oct 30 EO is widely cited as the most ambitious national AI safety governance in history, explicitly covering CBRN risk including nuclear.
- **Cyber and biosafety actions.** National Cybersecurity Strategy and biotech safety EO (2023) built a layered approach to non-nuclear existential risks.
- **Restraint on direct Russia conflict.** The administration maintained a consistent public line that U.S. troops would not enter direct combat with Russia in Ukraine, refusing to be drawn into escalation despite domestic pressure.
- **Israel–Hamas restraint.** Pressure on Israel for humanitarian pauses and civilian-casualty restraint during the Gaza war, while still supplying defensive systems.
- **AI voluntary commitments (July 2023).** 15 leading AI firms (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, Inflection, Cohere, etc.) signed White House voluntary commitments on safety testing, security, and trust — a pre-EO step toward shared risk reduction.
